policy.title: Policy-rate shock
policy.shockLabel: Change in the policy repo rate
qualitative: No India semi-elasticity of consumption to lending rates was found with a verifiable citation.
Interest-rate differentials can move portfolio flows and the rupee; no cited coefficient, and RBI FX intervention breaks any mechanical link.
An appreciation would lower imported inflation (see the rupee scenario), but the size of the rupee move is not modelled.
Follows only if the consumption link were quantified.

oil.title: Crude oil price shock
oil.shockLabel: Change in the crude oil price versus baseline
qualitative: A wider CAD adds to rupee depreciation pressure; size depends on capital flows and RBI intervention.

Under full pass-through the direct budget cost is nil by construction; in practice excise cuts or subsidies split the shock between consumers and the budget (only the full-absorption upper bound is cited).
Second-round effects (wages, expectations, monetary response) are not modelled.

rupee.title: Rupee depreciation
qualitative: Most Indian trade is invoiced in US dollars, so export prices in foreign currency may not fall at once; how far volumes respond depends on price elasticities, for which no India value was verified.
Oil, gold and capital goods dominate imports and respond weakly to price in the short run.

capex.title: Public capital expenditure
qualitative: Crowding-in: public infrastructure can raise the return on private capital (complementarity). No cited India coefficient is used here.
Crowding-out: more government borrowing can raise yields and compete for savings; size depends on financing and monetary conditions.
Higher yields would offset part of the crowding-in.

policy.label: Δ lending rate on fresh rupee loans (WALR)
assumptions: Pass-through ratio of the May 2022–Sep 2023 tightening applies to any shock, up or down.
Linear; no asymmetry between hikes and cuts; liquidity conditions as in that episode.

policy.label: Δ lending rate on outstanding rupee loans (WALR)
assumptions: Same episode ratio; slower than fresh loans because fixed-rate and MCLR-linked loans reset with a lag.

policy.label: Δ annualised nominal bank credit growth
assumptions: Estimated on 2001–2011 data (pre-EBLR); the source notes the effect weakened after the global financial crisis.
Lag of about seven months; ceteris paribus.

policy.label: Δ investment rate (investment / GDP)
assumptions: The change in the real interest rate equals the change in the fresh-loan lending rate: inflation expectations are held fixed (a simulator assumption, not from the source).
Source coefficient is for a 100 bps real-rate change, scaled linearly.

policy.label: Δ real GDP growth (via the real interest rate)
assumptions: As for the investment link: inflation expectations held fixed.
Covers the interest-rate channel only, not credit, exchange-rate or expectations channels separately.

policy.label: Δ headline CPI inflation (cumulative)
assumptions: Ratio from one episode (250 bps tightening, effect to Q2:2024-25) applied linearly to any shock.
Includes all channels the source's model captures; do not add it to the other links.

oil.label: Δ oil import bill at unchanged volumes
assumptions: Mechanical: volumes, the rupee and GDP unchanged (an accounting identity, not a behavioural estimate).

oil.label: Δ current account deficit as % of GDP (wider = positive)
assumptions: Mint Street Memo sensitivity at 2018-19 import volumes and GDP; today's ratio to GDP would differ.
Linear in US$ per barrel; growth does not offset (as the memo finds).

oil.label: Δ current account deficit in US$ (wider = positive)
assumptions: 2018-19 oil import volumes.

oil.label: Δ headline CPI inflation
assumptions: Full pass-through to domestic fuel prices (as in the source scenario).
Linear scaling of a 10% scenario to other sizes is a simulator assumption.

oil.label: Δ real GDP growth
assumptions: Full pass-through scenario of the source; linear scaling.

oil.label: Δ fiscal deficit, upper bound (full absorption)
assumptions: Government passes none of the increase to consumers (zero pass-through); the source calls this an upper bound.

rupee.label: Δ rupee price of imports
assumptions: Import prices fixed in US dollars (dollar invoicing, full pass-through at the border); a simulator assumption, exact by construction.

rupee.label: Δ headline CPI inflation
assumptions: RBI MPR scenario for a 5% depreciation, scaled linearly; the source finds pass-through is non-linear and asymmetric, so large shocks are less reliable.

rupee.label: Δ real GDP growth (export stimulus)
assumptions: RBI MPR scenario, short-term export stimulus; linear scaling.

rupee.label: Δ trade balance, short-run elasticities
assumptions: Elasticities approach, first order: export prices fixed in ₹, import prices fixed in US$.
Volumes respond with the stated elasticities; income effects and second-round price effects ignored.

rupee.label: Δ trade balance, long-run elasticities
assumptions: As the short-run link, with long-run elasticities. Holding the real depreciation constant over the long run ignores the inflation that erodes it.

capex.label: Δ nominal GDP
assumptions: Impact (within-year) multiplier from a structural model for the combined Centre and States.
Same multiplier for any size or sign of change; no supply constraints.

capex.label: Δ fiscal deficit before revenue feedback
assumptions: Exact identity: extra spending not matched by extra revenue adds one-for-one to the deficit.

capex.label: Δ fiscal deficit after revenue feedback
capex.equation: \Delta FD / Y = \Delta G / Y - \tau\,\Delta Y / Y,\quad \tau = \tfrac{\text{revenue}}{Y}
assumptions: Revenue rises in proportion to nominal GDP (unit buoyancy), a simulator assumption.
Ignores the change in the GDP denominator of the ratio (first order).
